adhere to.n: Adhere to is a formal verb phrase used for rules, standards, guidelines, deadlines and principles. You will see it in workplace policies and reports: staff must adhere to safety procedures. It suggests faithful, careful following rather than a loose attempt. A common learner mistake is to leave out the preposition and write adhere the rules; you need to after adhere. Do not confuse it with the physical meaning, where tape or glue adheres to a surface. Memory tip: picture a sticker that sticks to a wall, and your behaviour sticks to the rule in the same way.
x: All contractors are expected to adhere to the company's code of conduct.
The project failed because the team did not adhere to the agreed timetable.
Hospitals that adhere to the new guidelines see fewer infections.

anticlockwise.n: British English prefers this direction word; American English says counterclockwise. As an adverb it follows a verb of movement: turn the key anticlockwise, walk anticlockwise around the room. It can also work as an adjective before a noun, such as an anticlockwise rotation. The spelling anti-clockwise with a hyphen is also acceptable. A simple memory aid: clock hands go clockwise, and anything that goes the other way is anti, meaning against, the clock.
x: To loosen the lid, twist it anticlockwise until it comes free.
Athletes run anticlockwise on a standard running track.
Turn the dial anticlockwise to lower the volume.

archaeological.n: Anything linked to archaeology can be called archaeological, and the word goes before a noun: an archaeological site, dig, survey or find. It is more specific than ancient: it relates to excavation and the study of material remains, not just great age. You see it often in news about history and museums. Learners often misspell it. The stress falls on the fourth syllable: ar-kee-o-LOG-i-cal. To remember the middle, link -log- with study of, as in biology.
x: The archaeological team spent three summers excavating the hillside.
A major archaeological discovery changed what historians knew about the town.
The road was delayed because of an archaeological survey of the land.

artifact.n: Spelled artifact in American English and often artefact in British English, this noun means a human-made object that tells us about a culture, such as a tool, coin or pot. Museums display artifacts, and archaeologists record them. In computing it has a different sense: a file produced by a process. Do not use it for natural things like fossils or rocks, which nobody made. Memory tip: art + fact, made by human skill, and it tells us a fact about the past.
x: Visitors may handle a Roman artifact under the supervision of a museum guide.
The farmer dug up an ancient artifact while plowing his field.
Each artifact was cleaned, photographed and given a catalogue number.

astronomy.n: Do not mix astronomy with astrology: astronomy is the uncountable noun for the science of space, while astrology claims stars affect personality. Typical collocations include study astronomy, amateur astronomy and an astronomy club. The person is an astronomer, and the adjective is astronomical, which also means extremely large when talking about prices. The ending -nomy suggests laws, like economy, so think of the rules that stars follow.
x: She dreamed of working in astronomy ever since she saw Saturn through a telescope.
Our school has a small astronomy club that meets on clear evenings.
Modern astronomy depends on powerful telescopes in space.

axis.n: Axes is the plural of this noun, pronounced differently from the tool word axes. In science it is the line around which something spins, such as the Earth's axis. In charts and graphs, the horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis show the measured values, which is the sense you need when describing charts. Useful phrases are on its axis and along the axis. Learners often write axis for the plural; the correct form is axes. In politics it can also mean an alliance of countries, though that use is less common.
x: The Earth rotates on its axis once every twenty-four hours.
Label each axis clearly so the reader understands the graph.
The vertical axis shows the number of visitors per month.

a balanced approach.n: People use this phrase when advising that several viewpoints or needs should be weighed fairly instead of choosing one extreme. It often appears in essays and discussions: a balanced approach to diet, to tourism, to technology in schools. Typical verbs are take, adopt and need. The phrase is positive and sounds reasonable, so writers sometimes use it as a safe conclusion. A common mistake is dropping the article a, or forgetting to say what is being balanced. Memory tip: picture weighing scales with equal weights on both sides.
x: The council wants a balanced approach to housing and green spaces.
Teachers recommend a balanced approach, mixing screen time with outdoor play.
I think we should take a balanced approach rather than ban cars completely.

a compelling argument.n: Reasoning that makes readers feel they must agree is a compelling argument. Compelling means powerful and hard to ignore, so it is stronger than good or interesting. You can make, present or offer one, and others may find it hard to resist. It fits essays, debates and business meetings, and sounds more formal than a strong point. Learners sometimes say a compelled argument, which is wrong; the correct adjective ends in -ing.
x: The lawyer made a compelling argument for shorter working weeks.
She presented a compelling argument that changed the manager's mind.
There is a compelling argument for planting more trees in cities.

a knock-on effect.n: An idiom that describes an indirect chain reaction: one event causes a second, which then causes others. It is common in British English, news, business and economics, as in a knock-on effect on prices or on jobs. You usually have or cause a knock-on effect, and the phrase often takes the preposition on. It is not a physical knock, so avoid using it for a single direct result. The hyphen in knock-on is normal.
x: The factory closure had a knock-on effect on local shops and cafes.
A late train can have a knock-on effect on the whole timetable.
Raising fuel taxes may have a knock-on effect on food prices.

a small minority.n: Only a tiny share of a larger group does or thinks something, says this phrase. The normal pattern is a small minority of plus a plural noun, and the verb often agrees with that noun: a small minority of students prefer silence. It is common in reports and opinion writing, usually to say that a few people should not define the whole group. Learners mistakenly write a small minorities, or use it when the number is actually quite big.
x: Only a small minority of customers complained about the new design.
A small minority of drivers ignore the speed limit near schools.
Reports of bad behaviour came from a small minority of the fans.

a striking feature.n: Describing graphs, tables, places or people, this phrase points to a detail that catches the eye at once. Striking is stronger than interesting and suits data description, such as a striking feature of the chart is the sharp rise in 2010. You can also use a striking contrast, similarity or resemblance. The word comes from strike: something striking strikes your attention like a clock striking the hour.
x: A striking feature of the town is its brightly painted harbour.
A striking feature of the results was the gap between boys and girls.
A striking feature of the graph is the sudden fall in sales after July.

account for.n: This phrasal verb has two main meanings. One is to make up a share of a total, popular in data description: young people account for forty per cent of users. The other is to explain a reason: nobody could account for the missing money. In the passive, a missing person may be unaccounted for. Learners often drop for, or use it as accounts on. It does not mean to count money, even though it looks like accounting. Tip: both senses answer a question, either what part, or what reason.
x: Tourism can account for almost a third of the island's income.
How do you account for the sudden drop in sales this spring?
Rent and food account for most of a student's monthly spending.

acknowledge receipt.n: Business writers use this formal phrase to confirm that a letter, payment, parcel or email has arrived; it says nothing about agreeing with the contents. It is followed by of: acknowledge receipt of your letter. You will see it in offices, law and customer service, often as a polite request: please acknowledge receipt of this message. Learners sometimes say acknowledge the receiving, which is unnatural. An everyday alternative is to confirm that you got something.
x: Kindly acknowledge receipt of these documents as soon as they arrive.
We acknowledge receipt of your payment and thank you for your order.
The clerk asked us to acknowledge receipt of the parcel in writing.

address an audience.n: This phrase means speaking formally to a group, as at a lecture, speech or ceremony. Address is a verb with stress on the second syllable, and it takes the group directly: address the crowd. A real learner error is address to the audience, with an extra preposition. Related phrases include address the meeting and deliver a speech. It sounds more formal than talk to people, so it is less natural for a chat with friends.
x: The president will address an audience of two thousand students on Friday.
She felt nervous before she had to address an audience for the first time.
He will address an audience of local business owners about the new market.

advocate.n: As a verb, advocate means to publicly support an idea, plan or policy, and its ending is pronounced like the word eight. In formal writing it takes a direct object or an -ing form: advocate reform, advocate using public transport; advocate for is common in American English. Avoid advocate to do. The noun, with a weaker ending, means a person who supports a cause, as in an advocate of free education. The register is formal, common in news and academic writing. Tip: advocate shares a root with voice, so you give a voice to a cause.
x: Many doctors advocate regular exercise as a way to reduce stress.
The group advocates banning plastic bags in all local shops.
He has long advocated better public transport for rural areas.

aesthetic.n: Aesthetic usually comes before a noun and relates to beauty and artistic taste: an aesthetic quality, aesthetic value, an aesthetic choice. It says nothing about whether something is beautiful or works well, only how it looks. It also works as a noun, as in the minimalist aesthetic. The pronunciation is es-THET-ik in the US and ees-THET-ik in the UK. Learners often misspell it, and the American spelling esthetic is rare.
x: The architect cared as much about aesthetic appeal as about cost.
Many shoppers choose products for aesthetic reasons rather than practical ones.
The garden has a simple aesthetic that feels calm and modern.

after which.n: Use after which to link two clauses when the next event comes later. It follows a comma and starts a new clause, so it suits a process or sequence: leave the dough for an hour, after which you can bake it. The word which refers back to the whole previous clause. It is more formal than and then. Learners often leave out the comma before after which, or repeat the subject right after it.
x: Stir the mixture for ten minutes, after which you can pour it into a tin.
The meeting lasted two hours, after which everyone went home tired.
He studied abroad for a year, after which he returned to open a school.

algae.n: You will meet algae in ponds, oceans and aquariums, in phrases like green algae or an algae bloom. Science writing usually treats it as a plural noun, with the singular alga rarely used, though many speakers use it as a mass noun, so pick a verb that fits and stay consistent. Algae are not true plants because they lack roots, stems and leaves. Both AL-jee and AL-gee are heard; AL-jee is the most common.
x: Too much sunlight can cause algae to cover the surface of the pond.
Some scientists are studying algae as a possible source of clean fuel.
The fish tank turned green after algae began to spread.

allegedly.n: Journalists use this adverb to report a claim that has not been proved, which helps them avoid saying something is certainly true. It often sits before a verb or participle: the man allegedly stole the car, or an allegedly dangerous product. It is formal and commonly used in news and legal contexts. Learners sometimes treat it as meaning certainly, which is the opposite. Do not use it for things you personally know.
x: The company allegedly ignored several safety warnings before the accident.
He was allegedly seen leaving the building just after midnight.
The allegedly stolen painting was found in a storage room.

anecdotal.n: Evidence taken from a few personal stories or casual observations, instead of controlled research, is called anecdotal. It is often a polite criticism: the evidence is only anecdotal, so it may not be reliable. Typical partners are evidence, report, data and proof. The related noun anecdote means a short story about a real event. Learners mistakenly use it for any funny story, or think it means false; it only says the proof is weak or limited.
x: The claim rests on anecdotal evidence rather than a proper study.
Anecdotal reports suggest the new bus route has saved people time.
Her anecdotal account was interesting, but it proved nothing on its own.

anomaly.n: An anomaly is something that departs from the usual pattern or what you would expect, often in data, science or behaviour. It can be a single odd reading in a table, or a strange result in an experiment. Common patterns are a statistical anomaly, detect an anomaly and an anomaly in the data. The plural is anomalies, and the adjective is anomalous. It is neutral and more technical than strange or odd. Learners often stress the wrong syllable; say a-NOM-a-ly.
x: The scientists could not explain the anomaly in the temperature readings.
One year of very low rainfall looked like a clear anomaly.
The software flags any anomaly it finds in the bank records.

apprenticeship.n: An apprenticeship is a period of paid work combined with training, often lasting several years, in a trade such as carpentry, plumbing or cooking. Common verbs are do, start, complete and offer an apprenticeship. The learner is an apprentice, and the employer or master teaches the skills. It differs from an internship, which is often shorter and less formal. Learners often misspell it: the double p comes at the start (ap-pren-tice-ship). The ending -ship names a state, like friendship.
x: After school, she began an apprenticeship with a local electrician.
The company offers a four-year apprenticeship in engineering.
His apprenticeship gave him skills that a classroom could not teach.

archaeologist.n: A person who studies the human past by examining buildings, tools, bones and other remains, usually through careful digging and recording, is an archaeologist. The related noun is archaeology and the adjective is archaeological. American English also allows the spelling archeologist. Do not confuse the job with a historian, who works mainly from written sources, or a palaeontologist, who studies fossils. Learners often stress the wrong syllable: the stress falls on the third one, ar-kee-OL-o-jist. The start, arch, comes from a Greek root meaning ancient or beginning.
x: The archaeologist brushed the soil carefully from the broken pot.
A team led by a young archaeologist found the ruins of a Roman bath.
Being an archaeologist means long days of patient work outdoors.

architectural.n: Belonging to the world of building design and style, and it normally comes before a noun: architectural drawings, an architectural masterpiece, architectural details. It is related to architecture, the subject, and architect, the person. Writers use it for cities, tours and historic buildings. Learners sometimes confuse it with architecture itself, writing architecture features, which is not natural; use the adjective instead.
x: The old town is famous for its architectural variety and narrow streets.
Students studied the architectural plans for the new library.
Tourists come to admire the architectural beauty of the cathedral.
